title: Investigating the effect of VR-mediated pragmatics instruction on L2 refusal strategies
abstract: Pragmatic competence remains a vital yet often overlooked area in instructed second language learning, particularly in the domain of refusal speech acts. This quasi-experimental study investigated the effect of VR-mediated explicit pragmatics instruction on L2 learners’ refusal strategies. Fifty-two intermediate-level EFL Turkish university students were drawn from two intact B1-level classes assigned to experimental (N = 27) or control (N = 25) conditions. Inferential analyses were conducted on the 37 participants (experimental: N = 19; control: N = 18) who completed three testing phases. The experimental group received six hours of VR-based pragmatics training through ThingLink , a non-immersive VR platform, practicing refusal strategies in interactive virtual environments with immediate feedback, whereas the control group received traditional coursebook instruction that implicitly addressed pragmatics. Discourse Completion Tests elicited refusal responses across interlocutor status conditions, and performance-based tasks complemented the DCTs using an adapted pragmatics assessment rubric. Exploring AI-supported peer feedback in EFL writing: How do learners engage beyond the classroom?
abstract: This study explores how English as a Foreign-Language (EFL) learners engage with AI-supported peer feedback in informal digital learning contexts. Adopting the Technology Acceptance Model (TAM) and a three-dimensional model of engagement (affective, behavioral, and cognitive), the study investigates how perceived usefulness (PU) and perceived ease of use (PEOU) influence learners’ participation in AI-mediated peer review tasks. Using an explanatory sequential mixed-methods design, survey data were collected from 236 Chinese university students, followed by interviews with 18 participants. Quantitative results showed that both PU and PEOU significantly predicted engagement, with PU exerting the strongest influence, especially on cognitive engagement. Mediation analysis revealed that PEOU shaped engagement indirectly via PU. Qualitative findings highlighted that AI tools were perceived as supportive in reducing peer pressure and promoting deeper revision strategies. However, concerns about irrelevant or overly generic feedback pointed to the need for developing students’ critical awareness of AI support. Culturally responsive instruction for writing courses in the UAE: Leveraging speaking skills for writing development
abstract: At English Medium Instruction universities in the Arab Gulf and broader Middle East and North Africa (MENA) region, there is a lack of research on the tensions between Western academic writing pedagogies and local epistemologies and cultural practices. This exploratory lesson that took place at an American style university in the United Arab Emirates, demonstrates an alternative approach to teaching academic writing by foregrounding speaking and presentation skills oriented toward more Culturally Responsive Instruction (CRI) operationalized here through the Culturally Responsive Instruction Observation Protocol (CRIOP) model. By changing a persuasive essay to a business pitch project, it enabled students to draw upon their creative, collaborative, and narrative competencies which are deeply rooted in Gulf Arab communicative culture. The students effectively engaged with the assignment and ultimately achieved the learning outcomes; however, it was found that some dissonance exists between pedagogical innovations that embrace a CRI approach and Westen oriented assessment practices. title: On legitimating translanguaging practices in secondary EFL classrooms: Presence, function and institutional standing
abstract: Implementation of pedagogical translanguaging in monolingual-framed secondary school systems is fraught with controversy. This study examines translanguaging practices in Poland and Azerbaijan, two post-socialist contexts where target-language-only norms coexist with linguistically diverse student populations. Drawing on a mixed-methods design comprising 38 audio-recorded English as a foreign language lessons across seven secondary schools, a teacher questionnaire, stakeholder interviews and document analysis, the study uses a presence–function–legitimation triad that asks where teacher-initiated translanguaging falls along a continuum from spontaneous translanguaging through planned translanguaging to pedagogical translanguaging , what functions it serves and whether it is legitimated as professional pedagogy. In Azerbaijan, overt teacher translanguaging was concentrated among a small subset of teachers and functionally confined to comprehension repair and behavioural regulation. In Poland, no oral teacher-produced episodes were identified, though covert multilingual scaffolding was present. Global Englishes pragmatics in focus: Unpacking Taiwan's ELT curriculum and textbooks
abstract: As Taiwan advances its agenda under the Bilingual 2030 policy, English is increasingly framed as a medium for intercultural engagement rather than merely an academic subject. With the expansion of English-medium instruction and English use in a variety of domains, Taiwanese learners are more likely to use English with other non-native speakers in global contexts. In this setting, pragmatic competence and Global Englishes Language Teaching (GELT), a framework with pragmatics at its core, are essential for enabling learners to negotiate meaning, manage interaction and adapt to diverse cultural norms in an increasingly multilingual and globalized world. Despite this policy shift, English Language Teaching (ELT) curriculum reform has not kept pace. This study examines the extent to which GELT dimensions are incorporated into Taiwan's national ELT curriculum guidelines and four widely used elementary English textbook series. Using deductive thematic analysis and qualitative content analysis across eight dimensions of an adapted GELT framework, the findings reveal a significant divergence between policy-level intentions and their realization in instructional materials. title: Reconceptualizing pragmatic competence in ELT: An ELF-aware framework for materials analysis and adaptation
abstract: Traditional approaches to pragmatic competence in English language teaching have emphasized conformity to native-speaker norms from Inner Circle Englishes, an orientation that proves inadequate for English as a lingua franca (ELF) contexts where communicative success depends on interactional flexibility, accommodation and negotiation rather than adherence to fixed standards. This study addresses this gap by operationalizing a reconceptualization of pragmatic competence through the ELF-Aware Materials Checklist, a criterion-referenced tool that enables teachers to critically evaluate and adapt materials for global English contexts. The framework is structured around three interconnected components − awareness of language and language use, awareness of instructional practices and awareness of learning − each examined through four universal criteria of authenticity, variety, relevance and reflection. The study investigates how the Checklist functions as both a pedagogical and professional development tool by addressing two research questions: how Checklist-informed lessons promote learners’ pragmatic awareness for global communication; and how engagement with the Checklist supports te

title: Enhancing EFL students' argumentative writing with collaborative argument mapping in the GenAI era
abstract: English as a foreign language (EFL) teachers now face a growing conundrum. Although generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) can assist learners in producing fluent text, overreliance on GenAI may risk undermining students’ independent writing development. The present study investigated the effect of collaborative argument mapping (CAM), a non-GenAI pedagogical scaffold, on EFL learners’ argumentative writing. Adopting a mixed-methods research design, we integrated Kialo Edu, an online CAM platform, into the argumentative writing instruction for 50 Chinese postgraduate EFL students. Repeated measures analysis of variance showed no significant improvement in students’ writing scores; however, a significant improvement in global cohesion was revealed. Further, students reported: (a) strengthened critical thinking and argument structuring; (b) generally positive platform experiences that clarified relations among claims, reasons, and evidence; and (c) more deliberate writing processes. Nevertheless, they also noted some challenges (e.g., information load, uneven attention to language forms). title: ‘It's everywhere’: experienced teachers’ principled orientation to ELF pragmatics
abstract: This paper explores how experienced English language teachers conceptualise and enact pragmatics, with particular attention to English as a lingua franca (ELF) perspective. Drawing on qualitative data from semi-structured interviews and a follow-up focus group with three experienced teachers enrolled on a UK-based MA in Applied Linguistics/TESOL, the study investigates: (1) how teachers understand pragmatics and position its importance within teacher expertise; (2) how pragmatics features in teacher education trajectories; and (3) how pragmatic awareness is enacted in classroom practice. Using reflexive thematic analysis, the findings reveal that teachers display principled orientation towards (ELF) pragmatics: it is widely recognised by teachers as essential for communicative competence, yet its conceptualisation and pedagogical implementation remain uneven. Participants reported limited exposure to pragmatics in initial teacher education and described encountering the concept more substantially only during postgraduate study or exam preparation teaching. ‘Make the diversity of the language come alive’: Impacting pre-service teachers’ intentions to apply Global Englishes Language Teaching
abstract: This exploratory qualitative study investigated pre-service teachers’ intentions to enact Global Englishes Language Teaching after engaging in the Global Empowerment Project, an overseas teaching and service-learning program. This is important because the prevalence of global Englishes renders a traditional, first-language-normative approach to English language teaching inadequate since it does not reflect authentic English communication. Eleven Hong Kong-based participants traveled to Indonesia where they taught English and worked with international peers on a community service project. Thematic analysis applied to their written reflections suggested that the Global Empowerment Project experience enhanced participants’ intentions to include Global Englishes Language Teaching in their future teaching. Three interconnected themes influenced these intentions: authentic global Englishes communicative experiences, awareness raising about global Englishes, and a concomitant change in attitudes towards standardized and global Englishes varieties. title: Deployment of verbal-gestural intersemiosis in EFL teachers’ discourse: a systemic functional multimodal discourse analysis approach
abstract: With mounting recognition of the multimodal nature of teacher discourse, teachers’ deployment of semiotic resources such as the verbal and gestural modes is considered important in meaning making, and impactful to the students. Previous studies on pedagogic gestures tend to focus on gestures per se , while how they make meanings in orchestration with the verbal mode receives less scholarly attention. To examine the meaning-making mechanisms of teachers’ verbal-gestural orchestration and their pedagogical values in English as a foreign language (EFL) teaching, the present study adopts a systemic functional multimodal discourse analysis approach to explore how verbal-gestural intersemiosis can be designed to achieve intended pedagogy in Chinese EFL classrooms. The meaning patterns identified are discussed in relation to their realising forms. National top-prize-winning EFL teachers’ multimodal discourse were carefully examined based on a newly integrated framework that bridges the two modes in ideational meaning making. title: Forging Global Englishes pragmatic competence in the era of artificial intelligence
abstract: In recent decades, the fields of applied linguistics and language education have encountered a multilingual turn in which both educators and learners are encouraged to address and utilize pragmatic strategies for authentic intercultural communication rather than aiming to adopt native-oriented fixed standards. The incorporation of Global Englishes (GE) pragmatic strategies into English language education (ELE) requires the collaboration of policymakers, language educators, learners, and parents to move beyond language instruction confined to the classroom. To accomplish this, it is essential to overcome both ideological and pedagogical barriers in ELE. This viewpoint essay addresses key issues related to developing GE pragmatic competence in the era of artificial intelligence (AI) by focusing on the following topics: (1) integrating GE pragmatic competence into pedagogy and curricula; (2) rethinking assessment through GE pragmatic competence and AI awareness; (3) recognizing translanguaging as a pragmatic resource for inclusive communication; (4) readdressing locality in intercultural communication; and (5) developing critical AI literacy for GE pragmatic competence. title: Translanguaging for critical multilingual language awareness: Classroom activities for socially just language education
abstract: This article introduces a Translanguaging for Critical Multilingual Language Awareness (TL-for-CMLA) approach and illustrates how it can be operationalized through concrete pedagogical activities in language teacher education and additional language classrooms. The paper argues for an explicitly critical orientation that foregrounds power, racialization, and linguistic hierarchies rather than treating multilingualism as a neutral resource. The purpose of this innovation in practice article is to present two classroom activities that bridge critical language ideologies and everyday teaching practice in English as a Second Language (ESL) and Kindergarten-Grade 12 (K-12) classrooms with multilingual learners. The first activity uses multilingual versions of Little Red Riding Hood to develop metalinguistic awareness and challenge target-language only assumptions. The second activity centers multilingual, identity focused spoken word poetry to engage learners affectively, critically, and multimodally with questions of language, identity, and belonging. title: Enhancing English Public Speaking Self-Efficacy and Performance Through a CDIO-Based English Course
abstract: This study investigates the impact of integrating the Conceive–Design–Implement–Operate (CDIO) framework into English public speaking (EPS) instruction for English as a foreign language (EFL) university students in Taiwan. EPS has been widely recognized as a critical competence in academic and professional contexts, yet EFL learners often struggle with anxiety, limited practice opportunities and low self-efficacy. To address these challenges, the study implemented a quasi-experimental design with two Freshman English classes: a control group receiving traditional presentation training; and an experimental group engaged in a CDIO-based presentation training. Over an 18-week semester, students’ self-efficacy was measured using a validated EPS self-efficacy scale, while performance was evaluated with a rubric assessing language use, content, organization and delivery. Pre-test results showed no significant differences between groups, ensuring baseline equivalence. Post-test findings revealed that the experimental group demonstrated significantly higher self-efficacy, as well as superior performance in content development, organizational structure and delivery techniques. title: Conceptualizing and assessing competence in English as a lingua franca context
abstract: While the field of English as a lingua franca (ELF) has been growing, there is currently no assessment that fairly captures the nature of ELF communication. The necessity for such an assessment has been emphasized by some scholars, but concrete efforts to develop one have been slow. To stimulate discussion and evidence gathering, this thematic review examines ELF within the framework of communities of practice, highlighting key components of the theory to underscore the importance of learning in and through practice within these communities. The discussion then turns to indigenous criteria − that is what members of communities of practice actually value when evaluating or assessing their peers − which is highly relevant in English for specific purposes assessment. In fact, many ELF studies can be classified as contexts for English for specific purposes. By reviewing studies that explore indigenous criteria, we can gain a better understanding of how domain or non-language specialists determine what is important for performance or communication within their respective communities, as well as how these criteria differ from those perceived by language specialists or applied linguists.

title: Using dynamic feedback from customized LLM-powered chatbots in EFL argumentative writing
abstract: With the growing use of large language models (LLMs) in English as a foreign language (EFL) teaching, balancing teacher control over instructional focus with students’ autonomy in using artificial intelligence chatbots while ensuring more dynamic interaction have become key pedagogical concerns. This article reports on an innovative teaching practice implemented in a foundation undergraduate English for Academic Purposes course, which featured interactive feedback, including chatbot-mediated dynamic assessment, delivered through two custom-built LLM-powered chatbots. The intervention aimed to support students’ argumentative writing with specific reference to argumentation quality and linguistic accuracy, through an iterative multi-draft process. Drawing on observation and critical reflection on this practicum, the article argues that customized LLM-powered chatbots can provide dynamic, instruction-aligned feedback at scale to scaffold EFL learners’ writing process, while instructors remain essential in the loop to address the limitations of automated feedback. The article concludes with suggestions for refining this approach in future practice.

title: Artificial Intelligence Pollution in Digital Environments: Mitigating Adverse Impacts on Language Education through Multiliteracies Integration
Between silence and speaking: Willingness to communicate and global competence in Japanese EFL classrooms
abstract: Global competence-oriented English as a foreign language (EFL) education in Asia increasingly emphasizes communicative participation in English, yet classroom silence continues to characterize university EFL classes. This study examines data collected from a focus group, questionnaire and Delphi study to explore Japanese university students’ perceptions of willingness to communicate (WTC) in relation to EFL education and global competence. Findings reveal that while students view active English use as essential for global competence, they simultaneously perceive such behavior as socially risky within the Japanese classroom context. Rather than reflecting a lack of motivation, confidence or engagement, low levels of classroom verbal participation emerge as a socially situated dilemma between global communication expectations and locally embedded interactional norms. The study further demonstrates that WTC cannot be equated with verbal output, but is better understood as a latent, context-dependent capacity that may or may not be enacted through speech. From a global competence perspective, effective communication entails the ability to interpret and adapt to interactional conditions

Emerging pragmatic awareness through engagement with Asian Englishes: A Global Englishes-informed classroom study
abstract: Responding to current interest in how pragmatic competence can be taught and assessed in Global English contexts, this study examines whether Global Englishes (GE)-informed classroom pedagogy can support the development of early pragmatic awareness in the absence of explicit pragmatics instruction. The study reports a re-analysis of classroom data from a GE-oriented module implemented in an Italian secondary school, in which learners engaged with Asian Englishes and other English varieties through presentations and reflective journals. Although the original module was designed to raise awareness of linguistic diversity rather than to teach pragmatics, the dataset provides insight into how learners attend to meaning, interaction and sociocultural norms across English-using contexts. The analysis is framed through the Adaptive Control of Thought–Rational (ACT-R) model, focusing on the emergence of declarative pragmatic knowledge as a precursor to later procedural development. title: Communication strategies in task-based interaction: An ELF-aware perspective
abstract: This study examines how English as a Lingua Franca (ELF) interlocutors employ communication strategies during task-based interaction and how these strategies relate to ELF-aware communicative orientations of intelligibility, adaptability, and multilingual–multicultural awareness. Ten university students learning English as an additional language completed a closed information-gap task. Interactional data were video-recorded, transcribed, and analyzed through a combination of distributional analysis and interactional analysis, and complemented by stimulated recall to examine learners’ strategic awareness. The findings show that, beyond commonly reported strategies, participants frequently engaged in co-creating messages, deconstructing complex information, and adaptive self-repair. These strategies enabled learners to collaboratively clarify meaning, adjust their linguistic production in response to interactional demands, and draw on shared multilingual resources. title: Assessing pragmatic competence in ELF spoken interaction: Analytic rubrics for a university programme
abstract: English functions as a widespread communicative resource which is protean − highly adaptable in form − and shaped by contingencies of context. This situated variability constitutes clear evidence that pragmatic competence is central in effective language use. Understandings of English as an emergent practice therefore inform the pedagogical and administrative framework of an English as a Lingua Franca (ELF) programme at a private university in Tokyo. Within this framework, departures from native-speaker norms are interpreted as expressions of the diversity of global English use rather than as deficiencies. Despite the importance of pragmatic competence for successful ELF interaction, its role in assessment within the programme has remained largely implicit, a limitation which forms the basis of the rationale for the present study. Accordingly, this study proposes a framework of analytic rubrics aimed at making pragmatic competence in speaking more overt and assessable, expressed through attention to three interrelated constructs: intelligibility; linguistic accommodation; and communication strategies. title: Intersections of religious identity and ethical dimensions in ESL teacher identity: A Malaysian case study
abstract: This qualitative case study examines the influence of religious identity on English as a second language (ESL) teachers’ identity in Malaysia. Coupled with the concept of transidentitying as a conceptual framework, this study applies the notion of ethical self-formation in language teacher identity (LTI) research to analyse how religious identity shapes professional ethics in ESL teachers’ professional identity. This study employed semi-structured interviews, observation data and document analysis to explore how ESL teachers navigate their professional ethics using their religious identity. The findings reveal that religious identity is a formative force in ESL teachers’ professional ethics in promoting fairness and inclusivity in ESL teaching, maintaining professional integrity, and building positive collegial relationships in workplace. Thus, this study offers insights for both researchers and educators regarding the complexities of ESL teacher identity in a multireligious setting such as Malaysia, and the need for culturally responsive training for ESL teachers to help them acknowledge and engage with these connections between religious and professional selves.

title: From pragmatic routines and children's books to global English pragmatic competence
abstract: This paper reflects on innovative pedagogical work conducted in English Language and Literature and Translation undergraduate courses offered in a university in China. In these courses, pragmatic routines were addressed through a corpus-informed Chinese translation of What Do You Say, Dear? , a picture book of manners featuring ordinary pragmatic routines embedded in fantastical scenarios, providing a playful yet contextualized entry point into critical discussions about language, culture and communication. In these activities, students follow a sequence of tasks required to complete possible translations while being invited to move between languages and semiotic systems, drawing on their translingual repertoires to negotiate meaning and justify choices. Rather than arriving at fixed equivalents, students are positioned as multicompetent users navigating between pragmatic norms. The pedagogical activity is designed purposefully to foster both contextualized language awareness and Global English pragmatic competence, with pragmatic meaning not modelled on monolingual ideals but constructed dialogically across languages.

From ‘Here I Am!’ to ‘Here I Am.’: University EFL teachers’ duoethnography with LLM-powered tools
abstract: As large language models (LLMs) and LLM-powered tools such as ChatGPT enter language classrooms, teachers face new opportunities and challenges in adapting their pedagogical practices. This study adopts a duoethnographic approach to examine how two university English as a foreign language teachers in China made sense of, negotiated and integrated LLM-powered tools over time. Guided by the cognitive-socio-technical framework, the analysis traces their experiences across cognitive, workflow and organisational levels through tandem writing and dialogic conversations. Findings reveal a four-stage trajectory, from initial excitement and early experimentation to critical reflection and balanced integration, showing how enthusiasm gradually gave way to reflective, teacher-led engagement. While LLM-powered tools enhanced efficiency and creativity, they also generated tensions related to academic integrity, teacher identity and institutional support. The study highlights the situated and developmental nature of teachers’ engagement with LLM-powered tools and underscores the importance of teacher agency, ethical awareness and institutional dialogue in supporting context-sensitive integration

title: Listening beyond comprehension: Towards a taxonomy of second language interactive listening skills
abstract: Listening in second language education has long been conceptualised and operationalised with an overwhelming focus on one-way, non-participatory listening. Although this is necessary for the development of cognitive dimensions of second language listening, it leaves a gap where learners are under-equipped for two-way, interactive listening, particularly the socio-interactional dimensions of ‘being listeners’. In this paper, we argue that the construct of listening for second language teaching and learning should include skills for interactive listening. We review prevailing taxonomies of second language listening skills that serve as the basis for reference standards, syllabuses and assessments, and highlight the under-representation and under-specification of interactive listening. We then draw on insights from conversation analytic research on spoken interactions and second language interactional competence, to shed light on the nature of listening and listener actions in interactions. title: Assessing the impact of the Common European Framework of Reference for Languages on policy and testing practices in Thai higher education
abstract: The application and impact of the Common European Framework of Reference for Languages have been observed worldwide, especially in testing practices, since its introduction in 2001. This is partly because Common European Framework of Reference-based policies have often used the framework's proficiency scales as a key indicator of success. Although the Common European Framework of Reference as policy is expected to improve current practices, there appear potential challenges that could undermine its effectiveness in particular contexts. This study reports on the case of the Common European Framework of Reference-based policy in Thai higher education, where an English Exit Exam has been imposed to verify the proficiency of graduates. To obtain a clear picture of how the policy has been implemented, the study analysed 12 sets of English Exit Exam materials from 12 institutions, 44 questionnaire responses from university lecturers and administrators, and 17 online interviews with practitioners who were involved in the development of English Exit Exams. title: Pragmatics and transcultural communication through English as a lingua franca
abstract: The deep connections between English, globalization and intercultural communication are now well established. Research in English as a lingua franca (ELF) has made clear that this is a multilingual use of English in which other linguistic and communicative resources are present and frequently a core part of the interaction. Furthermore, ELF studies have highlighted that pragmatic strategies are a central part of those communicative resources. Yet how to approach pragmatics within an ELF framework has not been straightforward. Cross-cultural perspectives comparing the norms of first language communication in relatively static communicative contexts have little relevance to the dynamic and fluid communicative practices of ELF. This has led scholars to adopt intercultural frameworks to conceptualizing and documenting pragmatics in ELF interactions in which cultures and languages, and the accompanying pragmatic strategies, are viewed as adaptable and hybridized. Nonetheless, there are limitations to such intercultural perspectives due to the range and complexity of communicative resources we see documented in the superdiverse settings of much ELF communication. title: Negotiating teacher agency in English for Academic Purposes writing instruction: A case study of a Bangladeshi early-career teacher
abstract: Research on teacher agency in language education has expanded, yet limited empirical attention has been given to how teacher agency is negotiated in the everyday teaching of academic writing, particularly by early-career instructors working in under-resourced higher education contexts. This exploratory single-case study examines how an early-career English for Academic Purposes instructor in Bangladesh negotiated teacher agency while teaching academic writing within a resource-constrained public university. Guided by an ecological perspective on teacher agency, data were generated through a classroom observation, three semi-structured interviews, a reflective diary and a student focus group, and analysed using reflexive thematic analysis. The findings show that teacher agency was enacted through situated pedagogical judgement, including curriculum pacing, epistemic mediation and constraint-aligned instructional recalibration, rather than through overt resistance or pedagogical innovation. In conversation with Andy Kirkpatrick: Teaching and assessing pragmatic competence in a global Englishes context
English-as-an-additional-language teachers’ identity and receptivity to feedback inspired by Global Englishes Language Teaching: A dialogical self theory approach
abstract: This study investigated how university English-as-an-additional-language teachers’ professional identity mediated their receptivity to Global Englishes Language Teaching-inspired feedback. Drawing on Dialogical Self Theory as an analytical framework, semi-structured interviews incorporating purposefully designed vignettes were conducted with 13 participants from both English major and non-English major programs at universities in China. Findings showed that participants’ multiple-identity positions create both barriers and pathways for Global Englishes Language Teaching innovation. Although institutional constraints and accuracy-focused traditions may have impeded change, cultural sovereignty emerged as a powerful catalyst enabling teachers to transcend native speakerism. Implications for Global Englishes Language Teaching-oriented teacher professional programs are discussed.

title: Modeling the associations among language teachers’ engagement, self-efficacy, and dispositions toward loving pedagogy
abstract: Teacher engagement is a critical factor in educational quality, yet the predictive role of recently introduced constructs like loving pedagogy remains underexplored. Grounded in self-determination theory, this study employs structural equation modeling to investigate the associations among English-as-a-foreign-language teachers’ work engagement, self-efficacy, and their dispositions toward loving pedagogy. Data were collected via electronic surveys from 289 Iranian English-as-a-foreign-language teachers. The findings demonstrated that both loving pedagogy and self-efficacy are significant determinants of teacher engagement. Notably, loving pedagogy was found to be a stronger predictor of engagement than self-efficacy. The results also revealed a significant positive relationship between teachers’ self-efficacy and their tendency toward loving pedagogy. This suggests that English-as-a-foreign-language teachers who adopt a pedagogy characterized by kindness, empathy, and acceptance, and who concurrently possess a strong belief in their teaching capabilities, are more likely to exhibit higher levels of cognitive, emotional, and social engagement. title: Google Flow for task-based multimodal language learning: Pedagogical applications and challenges
abstract: This tech review explores Google Flow, an AI-powered filmmaking platform, as a potentially transformative tool for multimodal language learning. By generating text, image, and audio-synchronized video, Flow can empower educators to create highly contextualized and personalized learning materials that highlight specific linguistic and pragmatic features. Furthermore, it may further shift learners from passive consumers to active content producers within task-based frameworks, fostering collaborative design and critical reflection. However, the platform presents distinct challenges regarding equitable access, technical reliability, and ethical concerns like deepfakes and cultural thinness. Ultimately, Flow serves best as a multimodal simulator requiring critical comparison, human oversight, and integration with authentic communication.
